newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt, EU make progress towards free trade deal.
newsitem.headline: Egypt, EU make progress towards free trade deal.

text.p: A long day of talks on an association agreement between Egypt and the European Union made some progress but the EU negotiators will have to consult their superiors again, the Egyptian negotiator said on Thursday.
The main stumbling block throughout the talks has been the quotas the EU imposes on Egypt's agricultural exports.
"They (the EU's quota offers) are coming up...We are bridging many bridges but there are still a couple of bridges to be built," negotiator Gamal Bayyoumi told Reuters.

Bayyoumi and his team spent 14 hours up to midnight on Wednesday with an EU delegation led by Peter Zangel, the European Commission official in charge of relations with the Mediterranean, the Near East and Middle East.
The target is an agreement which would eventually bring about free trade between Egypt and the EU in manufactured goods and services, but excluding free trade in farm produce.
Both sides have said they would like to have something on paper in time for a meeting of European and Mediterranean foreign ministers in Malta next month.

"I could have initialled an agreement last night but they (the European negotiators) have to go to a higher level. I don't think they have the mandate (to reach a deal)," Bayyoumi said. Zangel was not available to comment on the talks.
Bayyoumi said that rather than tackling the quota problem head on, the negotiators were exploring the possibility of amending the draft agreement in peripheral areas.
"There are a lot of trade-offs and we are trying to find areas of flexibility," he said.

Areas for possible compromise include expanding the list of agricultural products Egypt can export to Europe freely, extending the seasons for duty-free Egyptian exports and reducing the EU's "entry prices" for produce, he added.
Bayyoumi declined to say what quotas the EU was now offering for the main categories -- rice, potatoes, citrus fruit and cut flowers. "It would be damaging to both sides," he said.
He added that visits to Cairo by the Belgian and Dutch foreign ministers over the next few weeks could be opportunities to advance the negotiations.
